message.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Loss of tooth or enamel is widespread in multiple mammal lineages. Although several studies have been reported, the evolutionary mechanisms of tooth/enamel loss are still unclear. Most previous studies have found that some tooth-related genes have been inactivated in toothless and/or enamel-less mammals, such as
                    <jats:italic>ENAM</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>ODAM</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>C4orf26</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>AMBN</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>AMTN</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>DSPP</jats:italic>
                    , etc. Here, we conducted evolutionary analyses on
                    <jats:italic>ACPT</jats:italic>
                    playing a key role in amelogenesis, to interrogate the mechanisms. We obtained the
                    <jats:italic>ACPT</jats:italic>
                    sequences from 116 species, including edentulous and enamel-less mammals. The results shows that variant ORF-disrupting mutations were detected in
                    <jats:italic>ACPT</jats:italic>
                    coding region among nine edentulous baleen whales and three enamel-less taxa (pygmy sperm whale, aardvark, nine-banded armadillo). Furtherly, selective pressure uncovered that the selective constraints have been relaxed among all toothless and enamel-less lineages. Moreover, our results support the hypothesis that mineralized teeth were lost or degenerated in the common ancestor of crown Mysticeti through two shared single-base sites deletion in exon 4 and 5 of
                    <jats:italic>ACPT</jats:italic>
                    among all living baleen whales.
                    <jats:italic>D</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>N</jats:sub>
                    /
                    <jats:italic>d</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>S</jats:sub>
                    values on transitional branches were used to estimate
                    <jats:italic>ACPT</jats:italic>
                    inactivation records. In the case of aardvark, inactivation of
                    <jats:italic>ACPT</jats:italic>
                    was estimated at ~23.60–28.32 Ma, which is earlier than oldest aardvark fossil record (
                    <jats:italic>Orycteropus minutus</jats:italic>
                    , ~19 Ma), suggesting that
                    <jats:italic>ACPT</jats:italic>
                    inactivation may result in degeneration or loss of enamel. Conversely, the inactivation time of
                    <jats:italic>ACPT</jats:italic>
                    estimated in armadillo (~10.18–11.30 Ma) is later than oldest fossil record, suggesting that inactivation of
                    <jats:italic>ACPT</jats:italic>
                    may result from degeneration or loss of enamel in these mammals. Our findings suggested that different mechanisms of degeneration of tooth/enamel might exist among toothless and enamel-less lineages during evolution. Our study further considered that
                    <jats:italic>ACPT</jats:italic>
                    is a novel gene for studying tooth evolution.
                  </jats:p>
title: ACPT gene is inactivated in mammalian lineages that lack enamel or teeth
